cf.title: improving handling of FPIs during recovery prefetching

input.subject: improving handling of FPIs during recovery prefetching

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal or the basic design. Three fixable level 2 points remain: maintenance-fit-2 (no measurement of the lookup cost for replay that gains nothing), replication-ondisk-1 (the squashed commit ties the fix to a catalog change, so it cannot be back-patched as is), and standards-compat-2 (the skip_fpi name). Message #1 shows demand from a field report and an earlier patch. Confidence is medium because the code was not read and a simpler alternative is expected but not posted.

brief.title: Skip recovery prefetches for blocks restored from a pending FPI
brief.problem: recovery_prefetch still issues prefetches for a block after an earlier WAL record carries its full page image, though replaying the FPI installs the page with no read. On replicas with IOPS limits this unneeded I/O inflates replay lag, and it hurts sync replication when the walreceiver reconnects and the startup process must first apply the backlog.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds a separate history of pending FPIs in the WAL prefetcher, a set-associative cache keyed by a hash of the block. Entries whose LSN is before replaying_lsn count as empty, and the cache is sized from the look-ahead distance (maintenance_io_concurrency times a multiplier). The prefetcher skips blocks found in the history; the nine patches would be squashed into one commit.
user_visible_surface: New bigint column skip_fpi in the pg_stat_recovery_prefetch view, documented in monitoring.sgml; the author calls the name provisional and easy to confuse with skip_fpw.
author_claims: The reproducer UPDATE touches every page, and the standby then prefetches pages that the FPI replay will overwrite.
The blog's 16x IOPS amplification comes from 128K read-ahead on the primary versus 8K reads on the standby.
The FPI history uses at most about 400kB at maintenance_io_concurrency=1000, and there is only one per instance.
The author could not build a case where the history lookup adds measurable CPU overhead.
brief.thread_state: Jan Nidzwetzki confirmed check-world passes and that posix_fadvise() calls dropped from 23,502 to 821 in a crash recovery test; Shihao Zhong posted a TAP test, now at v3 and approved by Jan. Tomas then said Thomas Munro may post a simpler alternative, so review of this series is on hold.
unclear: The material does not show Thomas Munro's alternative design or when it will arrive.
No one has measured the CPU cost of the history lookup in recovery without FPIs.
Shihao's suggestion to also track BKPBLOCK_WILL_INIT blocks got no answer from the author.
The thread does not address problem (2), the walreceiver restart behaviour, which the author calls the real issue.
No patch posted for back branches, though the author treats the behaviour as causing outages.

objections.title: Lookup cost on every block reference is unmeasured
objections.failure_scenario: A standby that replays mostly non-FPI records, with prefetch already working well, now does a hash and a group scan for each block reference whenever any FPI is pending. If that cost adds up, replay gets slower on standbys that never had the IOPS problem. The project finds out from user reports after release.
objections.argument: In message #6 the author asks others to check the CPU cost for normal cases and says he could not build a bad case himself. Jan's numbers in message #3 only count posix_fadvise() calls on the workload that gains from the patch. Patch 0009 exits early only when no FPIs are pending, which is rare right after a checkpoint, and the history can grow to about 400kB at maintenance_io_concurrency=1000.
objections.author_must_show: How much does replay throughput change on a CPU-bound standby with few useful skips, at default and high maintenance_io_concurrency?

critic.reasoning: In message #6 the author asks for this measurement and says nobody has done it. Jan's numbers count posix_fadvise() calls only on the workload that gains from the patch.

objections.title: Stats column ties an outage fix to master only
objections.failure_scenario: An operator on Postgres 15 to 19 runs a replica under an IOPS limit and keeps seeing replay lag after a walreceiver restart. The squashed commit changes pg_proc.dat and system_views.sql, which needs a catversion bump, so it cannot go to back branches as one commit. The operator finds out only when the fix ships in a future major release.
objections.argument: Message #1 links recovery_prefetch to outages, but the only stated way out on released branches is recovery_prefetch = off. Patch 0002 mixes the behaviour change with the skip_fpi column in pg_stat_recovery_prefetch and a changed function in pg_proc.dat, and the plan squashes all nine patches into one commit. A committer would likely ask for the in-memory FPI history to be split from the catalog-visible counter, so the history alone can be backpatched.
objections.author_must_show: Is the FPI history meant for back branches, and if so, can it ship without the skip_fpi column and the pg_proc.dat change?

critic.reasoning: The thread does not say whether a back-patch is intended, and a pg_proc.dat change cannot go to stable branches. Performance fixes are often master-only, so this stands as a question about patch split and has no bearing on the design.

objections.title: skip_fpi sits next to skip_fpw with a confusingly similar meaning
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA reading pg_stat_recovery_prefetch sees skip_fpw and skip_fpi side by side and sums them, or graphs the wrong one. After release, monitoring tools hard-code the column name, and renaming it later breaks their queries.
objections.argument: The 0002 commit message says the name "is not very self-explanatory" and "easy to confuse with skip_fpw", and nothing in the thread picks a better one. Both columns count blocks skipped because of a full page image, one for the record that carries it and one for later records. View column names become part of the monitoring contract once released, so a committer would likely ask for the name and the doc text to be settled before commit.
objections.author_must_show: What column name and documentation wording make the difference from skip_fpw clear to someone who reads only the view?

critic.reasoning: The 0002 commit message itself says the name is easy to confuse with skip_fpw, and no message in the thread settles a name. Acknowledging the problem does not resolve it, and a rename before commit is cheap.

refuted.title: New skip_fpi column ties a likely back-patched fix to a catalog change
refuted.failure_scenario: Operators on Postgres 15 through 19 hit the replay lag and outages from the blog post. A back-patch of the squashed commit would change pg_proc.dat and system_views.sql on stable branches. Stable branches do not take catalog changes, so the fix either stays on master or needs a different patch, and those users stay exposed.
refuted.argument: Message #1 links the behaviour to production outages and calls it a regression in replay. 0002 mixes the stats column, which needs pg_proc.dat, system_views.sql and rules.out changes, into the same series as the behaviour fix. The author plans to squash all nine patches into one commit. The material does not say whether a back-patch is intended, and the brief notes that no back-branch patch exists.
refuted.author_must_show: Is the fix meant for back branches, and if so, will the skip_fpi column go in a separate master-only commit?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which makes the same back-patch point and adds the concrete request to split the FPI history from the counter.

refuted.title: New skip_fpi view column blocks a back-branch fix and fixes the counter's meaning early
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator on 15 to 19 has the outage from message #1 and waits for a minor release. The fix stays in master because 0002 changes pg_proc.dat, system_views.sql and rules.out. Later, a simpler design counts skips differently, and skip_fpi still has to keep its documented meaning.
refuted.argument: Message #1 presents the extra I/O as part of an outage, but no back-branch version is posted, and the counter is in the same patch as the behaviour change. The commit message for 0002 calls the name provisional and easy to confuse with skip_fpw. Message #6 says the prefetcher's original author may post a different design, so the counter's meaning is not settled yet. A committer would likely ask for the counter as a separate, later patch.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the skip logic be committed and back-patched without the catalog change, with the skip_fpi counter as a separate master-only patch once the design is settled?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. The added point about the counter's meaning is weak, because the documented meaning of skip_fpi does not depend on how the prefetcher finds the pending FPI.

refuted.title: Second skip cache next to recent_block, while a simpler design is expected
refuted.failure_scenario: The FPI history goes in beside the four-entry recent_block cache, each with its own sizing rule and its own reset rules. Then the simpler design from message #6 arrives, and the project has to keep, merge or remove the history. Later changes to reader repositioning must remember the history reset, and nothing fails loudly if they do not.
refuted.argument: Message #6 reports that the person who wrote the prefetcher has a simpler and better approach, and the author suggests holding review. Commit 0006 says the reset after XLogPrefetcherBeginRead() is "merely a precaution" today. A future caller that moves the reader mid-redo would depend on it, and the only sign of a mistake would be missing prefetches. Message #1 says recent_block may also be too small, so two overlapping mechanisms may need rework later.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should the project keep a separate FPI history beside recent_block, rather than one mechanism that also covers BKPBLOCK_WILL_INIT blocks as raised in message #2?

critic.reasoning: 0002 explains why the FPI history is separate from recent_block. 0006 and 0008 reset it whenever the prefetcher is reconfigured, including after XLogPrefetcherBeginRead(), so a future repositioning caller is covered, and the expected alternative is a timing matter the author already raised.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch changes which blocks the WAL prefetcher reads ahead during recovery on standbys and in crash recovery.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: 0002 changes pg_proc.dat and system_views.sql to add skip_fpi to pg_stat_recovery_prefetch.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-2: skip_fpi sits next to skip_fpw with a confusingly similar meaning

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #1 links the behaviour to outages on released branches, and the squashed commit includes a catalog change.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a second cache in xlogprefetcher.c with its own sizing and reset rules, plus a new view column.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The prefetcher does a hash and a group scan for each block reference while any FPI is pending.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: How much does replay throughput change on a CPU-bound standby with few useful skips, at default and at high maintenance_io_concurrency?
Is the FPI history meant for back branches, and if so, can it ship without the skip_fpi column and the pg_proc.dat change?
What column name and documentation wording make the difference from skip_fpw clear to someone who reads only the view?
Should the history also track BKPBLOCK_WILL_INIT blocks, as message #2 suggests, since redo reads no page in that case either?
Will problem (2), the slow restart of streaming after a walreceiver exit, be handled in a separate thread?

committability.owner_note: The author, Tomas Vondra, says in message #1 that he was involved in getting recovery_prefetch into PG 15. The owner must know the WAL prefetcher and the redo read path.
committability.liability: The owner signs for replay speed on every standby that uses recovery_prefetch, and for the meaning of the skip_fpi column once monitoring tools read it. A wrong skip costs a synchronous read and does not change replayed data.
committability.author_follow_up: The author wrote a nine-patch series within days of the field report and says he will hold review for a possible simpler alternative, which suggests he stays engaged.

priority.reason: Replicas under IOPS limits gain, and message #3 shows posix_fadvise() calls dropping from 23,502 to 821. The change is mostly in xlogprefetcher.c plus one view column; review cost is set to medium because no code was read and a simpler alternative may replace the series.

provisional_note: Without the code, the correctness of the eviction by replaying_lsn, the reset paths and the group overflow behaviour could not be checked. The expected simpler alternative is not posted, so no comparison was possible.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: I thought it would be better to add a POSIx_fadvise description for the recovery_prefetch parameter here, to distinguish it from the database functions.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The entry proposes adding a description of posix_fadvise to the documentation of the recovery_prefetch parameter, to set it apart from database functions. precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. None of the shown messages discusses the documentation change. The last messages cover a buildfarm failure on topminnow, which Thomas Munro traced to pg_walinspect rather than to the prefetch code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Index Insert Prefetching
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an index AM callback amprefetch, implemented for btree, that walks the inner pages of each index and prefetches the target leaf page before index tuples are inserted. The executor calls it for all indexes, and for whole COPY batches, behind a GUC enable_insert_prefetch.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas objected that the patch duplicates the btree descent code and its runtime work, and only helps index insertion. He suggested a general async execution model, where aminsert() returns a future that can wait on I/O. The author found the idea interesting but raised open questions about control flow and concurrency. The patch then stopped applying, and no new version appears before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't like this approach. It duplicates the tree-descend code, and it
also duplicates the work of descending the tree at runtime.

precedents_retrieved.title: prefetching for nestloop / indexscan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an ExecPrefetch executor callback so that a nested loop reads a batch of outer rows and asks a parameterized inner index scan to prefetch the matching heap pages. It is a small proof of concept limited to nestloop with an inner index scan, controlled by a new enable_nestloop_prefetch setting.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry because the patch was a quick experiment and he had no time to keep working on it. Before that, Andres Freund questioned the extra executor tree traversals and suggested passing multiple values down in one parameter, possibly as one ScalarArrayOps index scan. Peter Geoghegan supported that direction. The author agreed it looks like block nested loop join, which moves the work away from this design, and his cached-data benchmark showed about a 30% regression.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But
the patch was just a quick & dirty experiment, I don't have time to work
on this right now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Prefetch the next tuple's memory during seqscans
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_prefetch_mem() macro and uses it in heapam.c to prefetch the next tuple's memory during page-mode sequential scans. Tuples sit in reverse order on the heap page, and the author expected CPU hardware prefetchers to miss this backward access pattern.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch. After the heapgettup()/heapgettup_pagemode refactor, he could no longer show the earlier seqscan speedup, and Apple M1 and Power8 tests showed no gain. He also came to believe that modern hardware prefetchers detect backward access patterns, and he wants to benchmark this before resubmitting.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The problem I'm facing is that after Melanie's recent
refactor work done around heapgettup() [1], I can no longer get the
same speedup as before with the pg_prefetch_mem().

precedents_retrieved.title: Adding linux cachestat in file Readv and Prefetch
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses the Linux 6.5 cachestat() syscall in file reads and prefetch to collect page cache statistics for a file range. It also stops prefetching when recently evicted pages suggest memory pressure.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra doubted that per-file cachestat data from one 1GB segment detects memory pressure, and he disagreed that prefetching should stop under memory pressure. He also noted that the patch had no performance evaluation. Robert Haas agreed and said pg_prewarm should read what the user asks for, and the thread does not show why the feature is needed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm not sure I even agree with the idea that we should stop prefetching
when there is memory pressure. IMHO it's perfectly fine to keep
prefetching stuff even if it triggers eviction of unnecessary pages from
page cache.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Write visibility map during CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make CLUSTER and VACUUM FULL write the visibility map during heap rewrite, by having rewriteheap.c build VM pages alongside heap pages (bypassing the buffer manager) and flush them to smgr. It used its own simplified all-visible check, relying on HeapTupleSatisfiesVacuum() having already set hint bits; TOAST relations were left without a VM.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected to copying visibility-map implementation details into rewriteheap.c and to adding another copy of visibility-determination logic, which he said has proven hard to get right. He also questioned part of the motivation and pointed to related prior discussion that might share logic, especially for TOAST. The author did not respond to these comments for over two months, and the entry was marked returned with feedback.

visibility. It has repeatedly proven hard to get right in the past, and

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P10] and [P13] target the walreceiver restart problem, and [P18] adds fadvise to replay; none of their recorded reasons applies to FPI skipping. Message #1 cites a 2021 mention of FPIs, deferred as acceptable for v1, and a 2025 patch using the 4-entry recent_block cache, which this series includes as 0001 and extends.
The only user-visible change is one view column; no syntax, GUC, pg_dump or client behaviour changes, so the standards angle sees only the two fixable points above.

The FPI history lives only in the startup process's memory. The proposal changes no WAL record, page format or wire message, and the history is reset at reconfiguration and timeline switch. A wrongly skipped prefetch costs a synchronous read and does not corrupt data. Beyond the backpatch split, this angle finds no persistent or cross-node state to object to.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. The FPI history lives only in the startup process, and its memory is bounded by maintenance_io_concurrency, which ordinary users cannot change for that process. A wrong or missing entry only adds or skips an advisory prefetch and never changes the data that is replayed. The new skip_fpi counter in pg_stat_recovery_prefetch shows no more than the counters the view already has.
Two committers who know the area are engaged, so ownership is not a concern. The objections are about splitting the patch and showing measurements.

No existing feature does this job. Setting recovery_prefetch = off avoids the extra reads but drops all prefetching, and the 4-entry recent_block cache is too small for FPIs, as message #1 explains. Thomas Munro's simpler alternative (message #6) is not posted, so it cannot be compared.

The material shows real demand from independent sources: a public field report of outages tied to recovery_prefetch (message #1), an earlier report with its own patch about 18 months before, and the same concern raised in 2021. Jan's crash recovery test cut posix_fadvise() calls from 23,502 to 821 (message #3), and the user-visible cost is one stats column, so a demand objection would not hold.
